summary:
Huánuco stands under Peru's national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The provision applies in Huánuco as elsewhere, since the statute is national and carries no regional opt-out.

The IDEHPUCP legal analysis of 15 April 2025, written by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The institute finds that the restriction rests on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors.

An earlier stage of the same policy line is recorded in the Infobae Peru report of 20 February 2025. The congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that point. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private premises. SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. IDEHPUCP also records that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so a corrected document is not readily available to a trans visitor or resident challenged at a restroom door.

The national violence baseline, drawn from the annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia and reported by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023. The homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, twelve of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023.

One 2023 case is described in detail. Rubi Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, was kidnapped from central Lima in February 2023 by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so these killings cannot be prosecuted as hate crimes.
tangentialFactors:
The facilities restriction moved through Congress in two steps in 2025: a committee-stage dictamen approved unanimously on 20 February, then plenary approval on 2 April with the second vote waived. The February text carried exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities; the analysis of the enacted Article 5.1 reproduced by IDEHPUCP states the prohibition without those carve-outs, so a visitor should not assume an exception will be honoured at a restroom door.

Gianna Camacho's objection is operational rather than formal: a restroom ban enforced through DNI checks by private security means the practical test is a document inspection, not a legal proceeding. The same dynamic appears in the SmartFit resolution, where a private company set bathroom assignment from the sex recorded on the identity card and a consumer-protection body declined to intervene.

Recorded killings of trans women account for 30 of 54 TLGBI homicides in the 2020–2023 period and 12 of 19 in 2023, which makes trans women the consistently most affected group in the national totals. The proportion of homicides with no identified killer, 26 of 54 overall and 13 of 19 in 2023, indicates that a substantial share of these deaths remain unpunished regardless of motive.

The absence of sexual orientation and gender identity fields in the state's crime-registration systems means the absence of recorded hate-crime convictions cannot be read as an absence of bias-motivated violence. The Rubi Torres Silvano case was processed as an ordinary killing and extortion matter, with two arrests in March 2023, and no hate-crime charge was available.
localsOnly:
Residents of Huánuco who need gender identity recognised on official documents face a national process that IDEHPUCP describes as long, costly and invasive. Until that recognition is completed, the sex recorded on the DNI governs which restroom a person may use on private and public premises, and the 2025 statute now backs that assignment for public sanitary facilities.

A trans person who is refused a restroom, or removed from one, can lodge a discrimination complaint with the consumer-protection body, but SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 shows the route failing: the complaint against SmartFit was dismissed and the company's DNI-based bathroom assignment left intact.

Monitoring of violence against trans people in Peru is carried out by university and civil-society bodies rather than the state. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI at Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia produced the 2020–2023 homicide and violation totals, and Agencia Presentes reported them; the state's own registration systems do not record motive by sexual orientation or gender identity.

Because Article 5.1 of the April 2025 law is a national statute, its application in Huánuco's shopping centres, health facilities, transport terminals and municipal buildings follows the national text, and a local authority has no power to exempt those premises.
outOfScopeNotes:
None of the three sources contains Huánuco-specific content: each of them reports the national framework, national statistics or cases from Lima, and the reports themselves note that no department-level material is present. Whether the restroom provision has been invoked in Huánuco, and against whom, is not sourced here.

No locally sourced figures exist in this inventory for killings, assaults or police complaints against trans people in Huánuco; the 54 homicides and 170 violation cases are national totals for 2020–2023 with no department breakdown published in these sources.

The status of the February 2025 dictamen is resolved by the April 2025 statute, which the IDEHPUCP analysis treats as enacted. Whether the earlier bill's custody and accompaniment exceptions survived into the final Article 5.1 is not stated by the sources and remains unresolved.

The July 2023 complaint that triggered the bills concerned gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport, not an airport or terminal in Huánuco; no comparable incident in Huánuco is documented in this inventory.
